title: QUIC RFC 9000 Address-Pair Peer Connection-ID Policy
purpose: Describe the bounded runtime policy that binds consumed peer-issued connection IDs to one local/destination address pair, avoids reusing that connection ID after validated migration, and retires peer-issued connection IDs for address pairs that are no longer active.
design_summary: The peer connection-ID state records the path identity on which each peer-issued connection-ID sequence is actually used for outbound packets. Application-data send paths and validated migration promotion pass the selected path through the peer-CID selector before packet protection runs. The selector reuses a CID already bound to the same address pair, preserves an unused advertised CID as spare capacity, and refuses to promote a new address pair when no unbound or same-pair CID is available. When a validated migration becomes the active path, the selector emits RETIRE_CONNECTION_ID requests for peer-issued CIDs bound to other address pairs that are no longer active. NEW_CONNECTION_ID processing preserves a currently bound destination CID instead of preemptively consuming a spare CID on the old path before migration.
data_and_state_considerations: Address-pair binding is stored alongside the active peer-issued connection-ID sequence map and is removed when the corresponding sequence is retired. The binding key uses QuicConnectionPathIdentity, including remote address, local address, and ports, matching the runtime's existing path-state identity model. The current peer destination CID remains the packet-builder seam; selection updates it only at outbound use or path-promotion boundaries.
edge_cases_and_constraints: A spare NEW_CONNECTION_ID advertised after a CID is already bound to the active path is not used for active-path ACKs or later same-path sends unless selected for that path.
Validated migration with a spare peer-issued CID switches outbound packets on the migrated address pair to that CID.
Validated migration without a spare peer-issued CID leaves the original active path in place rather than reusing a CID bound to the original address pair.
Maximum-length peer-issued CIDs remain eligible for new address-pair selection.
Same-address-pair additional CIDs do not cause retirement of the earlier CID merely because the address pair remains active.
alternatives_considered: Treat CID receipt as CID use; rejected because RFC 9000's address-pair limit applies to packets sent with a connection ID, and preemptive receipt-time switching could consume a spare on the wrong path.
Keep only a single current CID without path metadata; rejected because migration needs to distinguish same-pair reuse from cross-address-pair reuse.

Broaden the slice into multipath scheduling or public migration APIs; rejected because the current runtime owns one active outbound path and this proof only closes the address-pair CID discipline tail.
risks: The binding model follows QuicConnectionPathIdentity and therefore does not claim broader address-only equivalence beyond the runtime's current path identity semantics.
The slice does not claim multipath support, public migration controls, or hosted interop success.
If future path identity normalization changes local/remote address treatment, these CID bindings must be reviewed with that path-state change.

supplemental_sections.heading: Boundary
supplemental_sections.content: This design covers peer-issued connection-ID selection and retirement for the single-active-path runtime. It does not alter locally issued route registration, stateless reset token handling, preferred-address migration, multipath, or public API migration support.
